title: Come back when you are taller
idea: A height mark on a doorframe means nothing until there is a second one above it. The page is the edge of a doorframe with one pencil mark already on it, dated the day the site began; hold still against the paint and a mark is pencilled for you with today's date, and the frame keeps it, so the piece only finishes when you return. The room beyond the door is as light or dark as your own hour.
look: warm off-white paint and brown pencil on a full-window canvas; italic Georgia caption fixed at the bottom centre, speaking to the visitor

title: Under the paint
idea: Nobody rubs out a height mark; they paint over it, so every one ever made is still on the frame, sealed between two coats. The page is the jamb from 0 seen close, and scrolling sands it back through ninety-five years of colours in widening rings, each coat giving up the initials and dates pencilled on it just before the same sanding takes them off. It ends at bare pine and the carpenter's figure for the door, and scrolling back up does not put anything back.
techniques: localStorage read from an earlier piece
look: cream and tan paint layers with wood beneath, full window; small Helvetica labels, a caption fixed at the bottom

title: A bit more
idea: A door left ajar at bedtime is a measurement too: the exact width of what a child is afraid of, agreed again every night. The same doorframe as 0 and 1, seen in the dark from the bed; you hold the door and drag it, and a small voice says more, less, a tiny bit less, until it says there, and then someone walks off down the hall. The agreed width is different each date and slightly narrower than the last, and about five years after the first mark it is nothing and you are told you can shut it.
techniques: the date as a slowly closing parameter
look: dark room with a strip of amber light, full-window canvas; italic Georgia caption low in the centre, as a spoken voice

title: No one in particular
idea: The height marks on the jamb were made one person at a time, with a name and a date; the sill was marked by everyone at once and kept nobody. The doorway of 0 to 2 handed to a surveyor: a cold measured section through the threshold, its hollow dimensioned to four decimal places, deepest off centre toward the latch because nobody walks through the middle of a door. Nothing moves; the depth is recomputed from the date and deepens by one footfall for your having opened it.
techniques: the date as a revision number
html table as a title block
look: navy line on pale grey, a measured drawing on a sheet; small monospace type, a table as title block, left-aligned

title: About three seconds
idea: The felt present is about three seconds wide, and almost nothing you make fits inside it whole. A sheet of warm paper asks you to write your name, by finger, pen or keyboard, and every mark lasts exactly three seconds, so the first letter has gone before the last is made and you never see all of it at once. A deliberate break from the doorway of 0 to 3, which was all about marks that stay.
techniques: text that answers how long you took
look: warm cream paper with dark plum ink, full-window canvas; italic serif caption low in the centre, speaking to the visitor

title: Now serving
idea: A queue only moves while you are not watching it, which means your number can only ever be called when you are not there to answer. A waiting room: a red number on a sign, a pink ticket in your hand four places behind it, a wall clock, and a notice asking you not to watch the display. Nothing happens for as long as you look; leave the tab or close the page and the count advances every fifteen seconds, shown only in the tab's label, and when you come back your number has been called, nobody answered, and you are holding a new ticket further back.
techniques: page visibility as the only input
document title as a second display
look: institutional mint green wall, black sign with red LED digits at the top, pink paper ticket at the bottom; bold uppercase narrow sans and Impact numerals, used only as signage and printing, nothing addressed to the visitor as a voice
first: the first piece that is funny, and the first whose only input is the visitor's absence: it changes only while hidden or closed, and uses the tab's label as a display

title: Still
idea: A screen cannot hold anything; what you call a still image is wiped out and painted again about sixty times a second, and exists only as that repetition. A black square on a white wall, with a gallery label beside it and, running across the wall and through the square, a figure for how many times it has been destroyed and remade since you arrived. Nothing else changes, and if you look away and come back the label admits that for those seconds it was not made at all.
techniques: canvas 2d cleared and repainted every frame
the frame count as the only content
figure turned to run down a tall window
look: pure black on pure white, one centred black square; giant ultralight Helvetica numerals spanning the whole window and inverting to white inside the square; a small third-person gallery wall label in plain Helvetica at the top right
first: the first piece whose subject is the screen's own redrawing: the only thing that changes is a count of frames, and the first to speak in the third person, as a museum label about itself

title: Your call is important to us
idea: A phone tree is built so that giving up is always your decision and never theirs, which is why every call in its records was ended by the caller. A putty-coloured desk phone on an orange desk: lift the handset and it dials a helpline whose recorded voice is a wordless mumble captioned on the phone's own display, whose departments transfer you to each other, and whose hold music always restarts from the top and gets more warped, crushed and gappy the longer you hold or the more keys you press. Hold long enough and you reach an agent for half a sentence, or closed offices if it is outside nine to five where you are; hang up and the display files it under ended by caller, resolved 0, and then the phone rings to ask how satisfied you were.
techniques: formant mumble as a recorded voice
async script as a phone tree
look: putty-beige plastic telephone on a burnt-orange laminate desk, grey-green LCD; bold Courier capitals on the phone's display in the upper middle, used as captions for an automated voice and as a call log, rounded sans only as key legends
first: the first piece that is mostly heard: generated music and a synthetic voice are the main material, and the first built as a branching script the visitor navigates with a keypad, and the first that is angry

title: By heart
idea: At night you do not walk through the room, you walk through your memory of it, and the fear is the few inches by which the memory is wrong. A bedroom seen from above with no words anywhere: turn the light off at the switch and cross to the bed, then get up in the night and cross back, and in the dark you are shown only a dashed drawing of the room as you remember it, which drifts, swims when you are frightened and was never quite right, while chalk appears only where you actually touch something. Each time the light comes back on it shows your footprints, where you hit things, and how far the room you were walking through was from the real one; things are moved while you sleep, the cat goes where it likes, and from the third night there is sometimes something standing in the room that is not there when you look.
techniques: top-down plan with circle and box collision
hold to walk, speed from reach
a remembered map that drifts from the true one
touch marks drawn only at contact
heartbeat driven by a fear variable
look: near-black with dashed violet outlines and icy chalk-blue touch marks, one orange and one green point of light; the lit room in cold slate blues; no text on the page at all and no typeface
first: the first piece with no words in it, the first you move a body through as a space with things to collide with, and the first that is frightening

title: The travel
idea: The pleasure of a button was never in what it did; it is in the few millimetres it goes down and the click at the bottom, which is why people press ones that are not connected to anything. One fat red key on an empty yellow page: it goes down under a finger, a cursor or the space bar, makes one sound landing and a lighter one coming back, and nothing whatsoever happens as a result. It counts nothing, remembers nothing and leads nowhere.
techniques: css box-shadow as the side of a key
press and release as separate events
generated key click, down and up
look: one tomato-red rounded key with a dark red side, centred on flat lemon yellow; no text and no typeface, no caption
first: the first piece with no consequence and no state: the gesture changes nothing, records nothing and is the whole content, and the first that is simply pleased

title: More ancestors than people
idea: Two parents, four grandparents, and the doubling never stops, so thirty-six generations back you are owed more ancestors than there were people; the only way out is that they are the same people, reached again and again by different routes. The page is a typeset proof you scroll down: you are one enormous blue disc, then each line doubles the marks until they are smaller than the screen can make, a single square is declared to stand for all of them, and the squares double until they run out too. Then the conclusion, the tree narrowing instead of widening, and a tombstone. Every figure is a power of two computed on the page; nothing is data.
techniques: html and css only for the drawing
repeating radial-gradient as exact counts of dots
a change of unit partway down
numbered proof lines with sticky margin notes
relation names written out with every great
mood: giddy, arithmetical, awed and a little smug
look: cobalt blue on pale pink, dots and squares in a column down the page; roman Palatino-style serif with old-style figures and small caps, set as a proof: a proposition at the top, a ledger of counts and justifications in the left margin, a tombstone at the end
first: the first piece built as an argument: a proposition, numbered steps and a QED, and the first whose marks change what they stand for partway through, a dot becoming a square worth a quarter of a million dots

title: Seen by Jo, Priya
idea: No group chat ends with a goodbye; it ends with something trivial that nobody answered, and nobody knows at the time that it was the last message. The page is the chat of five invented housemates and you, played from the day it was made: bins and butter, moving out, one good night at the pub, a date nobody can do, a baby, two birthdays, and at last a question about a takeaway. You can tap replies, type your own or heart a message, and early on they pile in; later the same effort buys a promise, then a thumbs-up, then someone starting to type and stopping, and the blank wall between conversations grows with the months between them. Whatever you say after the end only makes yours the last message.
techniques: free text input matched by keyword
a warmth variable with falling returns
vertical space proportional to the log of elapsed days
dates computed back from the day of the first visit
localStorage transcript that ages in real time
look: oat-coloured dotted wall, cream bubbles and pale moss for your own, dark teal header, names in terracotta, teal, plum and ochre; system sans; all text is chat bubbles in a centred phone-width column, spoken by characters to each other, with date pills and a small receipt line, no caption
first: the first piece with characters who talk to each other and answer what the visitor writes, the first to take free typed text, and the first where silence is drawn as distance: empty scroll in proportion to the time nobody spoke
